name: Chisel
title: Chisel, hardware written in Scala
intro: Chisel is a hardware construction language embedded in Scala. A Chisel program is a Scala program that builds a circuit. It does not step through that circuit the way a C or Python program steps through statements. When the Scala finishes, what remains is a module of wires, registers and operations, which a later tool turns into Verilog. The spelling below is the chisel3 API (UC Berkeley, now maintained as chipsalliance/chisel). These lessons do not run the examples: generating hardware needs a Scala build with the Chisel library on it, and the simulator calls have changed between releases.

lessons.title: A generator, not a program
lessons.summary: Scala runs once and leaves a circuit behind.

sections.p: You write Chisel inside an ordinary Scala program. Scala’s own if, for and val run while the circuit is being elaborated: they decide which hardware exists. They do not re-run on every clock. A println in Scala fires once, at elaboration. A Chisel printf is different: it is hardware, and it prints later, when a simulator runs the circuit.

Elaboration produces an intermediate form (FIRRTL) that a compiler lowers to Verilog. The Verilog is what you simulate in a Verilog simulator or give to a chip tool. The Scala source is the generator, not the netlist.

practice.q: When does the Scala in a Chisel generator run?
options: Once, while the circuit is being built
Only when the chip is fabricated
practice.answer: Once, while the circuit is being built
practice.why: Elaboration runs the Scala to decide what hardware exists. The circuit then runs on its own.

practice.q: What is the difference between println and a Chisel printf?
options: println runs once at elaboration; printf prints when the circuit is simulated
They print at the same time
printf runs at elaboration and println runs every cycle
practice.answer: println runs once at elaboration; printf prints when the circuit is simulated
practice.why: println is Scala. Chisel printf is a piece of the circuit.

practice.q: What does elaboration produce, before Verilog?
options: A Scala class the CPU executes every cycle
practice.answer: An intermediate circuit description (FIRRTL)
practice.why: FIRRTL is the circuit Chisel built. A later compiler turns that into Verilog.

practice.q: A Scala if around a connection decides what?
options: Whether that hardware is generated at all
Which input wins on each clock
practice.answer: Whether that hardware is generated at all
practice.why: Scala if is elaboration-time. It is not a mux. A mux is when, in the next lessons.

practice.q: Why does this course not run the examples?
options: Generating hardware needs the Chisel library, and the simulator API has changed between releases
practice.answer: Generating hardware needs the Chisel library, and the simulator API has changed between releases
practice.why: The chisel3 generator API below is stable enough to teach. Driving a simulation is a separate toolchain.

lessons.title: Modules and ports
lessons.summary: Module, IO, and a bundle of directions.

sections.p: Hardware lives in a Module. Ports are declared together as val io = IO(new Bundle { ... }). Each field is an Input or an Output. UInt(8.W) is an unsigned value, 8 bits wide. 8.W is the width. A width is part of the type of the wire.

Input is driven from outside the module. Output is driven from inside. Flip on a bundle swaps every direction, which is how a child module’s ports line up with the parent’s. Forgetting a direction, or driving an input from the inside, is an elaboration error.

practice.q: What is a Chisel Module?
options: A piece of hardware with ports
A Scala function that returns an Int
practice.answer: A piece of hardware with ports
practice.why: class Add extends Module describes a component. The Scala class is the generator for that component.

practice.q: What does UInt(8.W) mean?
practice.answer: An unsigned value, 8 bits wide
practice.why: UInt is unsigned. 8.W is the width. SInt is the signed form.

practice.q: Who drives an Input port?
practice.answer: Logic outside the module
practice.why: Input is the module’s view of a signal someone else provides. The body drives Outputs.

practice.q: In the adder, what does io.y := io.a + io.b build?
options: An 8-bit adder connecting a and b to y
A print of a and b
A register that stores the sum
practice.answer: An 8-bit adder connecting a and b to y
practice.why: + on UInt is hardware. := connects that adder’s result to the output port. There is no register unless you ask for one.

practice.q: Where are a module’s ports declared?
options: As separate Scala vars anywhere in the file
practice.answer: Together, as io = IO(new Bundle { ... })
practice.why: IO wraps the bundle so Chisel treats those fields as the module’s ports.

sections.p: := is a connection, not a Scala assignment you can update over time. io.y := io.a wires a to y. If the same sink is connected again, the later connection wins. That “last connect wins” rule is how Chisel builds multiplexers: a default connection, then a conditional one that overrides it.
A Wire is a combinational node you can name. It has no memory. Until something is connected to it, it is an error to read it. val sum = Wire(UInt(8.W)); sum := io.a + io.b names the adder’s result.
sections.code:
val sum = Wire(UInt(8.W))
sum := io.a + io.b
io.y := sum

sections.p: 1.U is an unsigned literal one. 1.U(8.W) is that one, 8 bits wide. true.B and false.B are Bool literals. A bare Scala 1 is not a hardware value; the .U is what makes it one.

practice.q: What does := mean?
options: Connect a hardware source to a sink
practice.answer: Connect a hardware source to a sink
practice.why: := is a wire. It is not the assignment you use to change a Scala variable over time.

practice.q: Two connections drive the same wire. Which one is kept?
practice.answer: The later one
practice.why: Last connect wins. Conditional overrides of a default connection are how muxes get built.

practice.q: What does a Wire remember between clocks?
practice.answer: Nothing; it is combinational
practice.why: A Wire is a name for a combinational result. Memory is a Reg.

practice.q: Which of these is a hardware literal?
practice.why: The .U turns a Scala number into a Chisel unsigned literal. A bare 1 is only a Scala Int.

practice.q: What is wrong with reading a Wire that nothing drives?
options: It has no source, so elaboration should reject it
It reads as the last clock’s value
It prints a warning and continues
practice.answer: It has no source, so elaboration should reject it
practice.why: A Wire is not a register and it does not default to zero. Something must be connected to it.

lessons.title: Registers
lessons.summary: Reg and RegInit update on the clock.

sections.p: A Reg is state. The connection r := r + 1.U does not change r during elaboration. It builds an adder from the register’s output back to its input. The register captures that result on the clock. A Module has an implicit clock and reset.
RegInit(0.U(8.W)) resets to zero. A plain Reg(UInt(8.W)) has no specified reset value. The value you pass to RegInit is the reset value, not a value that updates when the Scala runs.

On the right-hand side, r means the value stored now, the output of the register. The left-hand side is the input, what will be stored at the next clock. So r := r + 1.U is a counter, not an infinite Scala loop.

practice.q: When does r := r + 1.U change the stored value?
options: On the clock, in the circuit
Immediately, as the Scala line runs
Never; + is not allowed on a Reg
practice.answer: On the clock, in the circuit
practice.why: The Scala line builds the adder and the connection. The register updates when the clock edge arrives.

practice.q: What does RegInit(0.U(8.W)) set?
options: A Scala var that starts at 0 and grows during elaboration
practice.answer: The reset value, an 8-bit zero
practice.why: RegInit takes the value the register holds when reset is asserted.

practice.q: On the right-hand side of r := r + 1.U, what is r?
options: The value currently stored in the register
The value about to be stored
practice.answer: The value currently stored in the register
practice.why: Reading a Reg yields its output. Writing it sets the input that will be captured next.

practice.q: How is a Reg different from a Wire?
options: A Reg holds state across clocks; a Wire does not
A Wire holds state; a Reg does not
A Reg can only be 1 bit
practice.answer: A Reg holds state across clocks; a Wire does not
practice.why: Registers are the memory. Wires are names for combinational results.

practice.q: Where do a Module’s clock and reset come from?
options: You must declare them as ordinary Inputs named clock and reset in every bundle
From the width of the first UInt
practice.answer: They are implicit on Module
practice.why: Module provides clock and reset. You can use an explicit clock if you need a second one, but the simple counter does not declare them in io.

sections.p: when is a hardware condition. The test is a Chisel Bool, and both branches exist in the circuit. otherwise is the other input of the mux. elsewhen adds another.

sections.h: Scala if is the other tool
sections.p: A Scala if runs at elaboration, on a Scala Boolean. Use it to decide whether to generate a piece of hardware (“if this parameter is true, add a register”). Use when when the choice depends on a signal in the circuit. Writing if (io.en) does not compile: io.en is hardware, not a Scala Boolean.
Inside when, a connection overrides the default only on the cycles where the condition is true. A common pattern is a default io.y := 0.U, then when(io.en) { io.y := io.a }.

practice.q: What does when(io.en) build?
options: A multiplexer chosen by the signal en
Hardware that exists only if en is a Scala true
A register enable with no mux
practice.answer: A multiplexer chosen by the signal en
practice.why: when is hardware. Both the true and the false connections are in the circuit, and en selects.

practice.q: Why does if (io.en) fail?
options: io.en is a Chisel Bool, not a Scala Boolean
if is not a Scala keyword
practice.answer: io.en is a Chisel Bool, not a Scala Boolean
practice.why: Scala if wants a Boolean known at elaboration. A port is a signal. The hardware conditional is when.

practice.q: What is otherwise?
options: The other input of the when mux
A Scala else that deletes hardware
practice.answer: The other input of the when mux
practice.why: when { }.otherwise { } is the two-way mux. elsewhen adds further conditions.

practice.q: A default connection, then a when that connects the same wire. When the condition is false, what is driven?
practice.answer: The default
practice.why: The when overrides the default only while its condition is true. Last-connect-wins is conditional here.

practice.q: You want a register only if a Scala parameter includeReg is true. Which do you use?
options: RegInit alone, which checks the parameter
practice.answer: A Scala if
practice.why: includeReg is known when the generator runs. Scala if includes or omits the register. when would put a mux in the circuit instead.

lessons.title: Mux and switch
lessons.summary: Named multiplexers, and a multi-way case.

sections.p: Mux(sel, in1, in0) is the same two-way choice as when, written as an expression. When sel is true you get in1; otherwise in0. MuxCase and MuxLookup build wider muxes from a default and a list of conditions or keys.
sections.code:
val y = Mux(io.en, io.a, io.b)
val z = MuxLookup(io.sel, 0.U)(
  Seq(0.U -> io.a, 1.U -> io.b, 2.U -> io.c)
)

sections.p: switch (io.sel) { is (0.U) { ... } is (1.U) { ... } } is a multi-way when. Each is arm may connect sinks; last-connect-wins still applies. Prefer Mux when you need a value in an expression, and switch when each arm does several connections.

practice.q: What does Mux(sel, in1, in0) return when sel is true?
practice.answer: in1
practice.why: The true arm is the middle argument; the false arm is the last.

practice.q: When is Mux a better fit than when?
options: When you need the chosen value as an expression
When you want to omit hardware at elaboration
When sel is a Scala Boolean
Never; they cannot express the same circuit
practice.answer: When you need the chosen value as an expression
practice.why: Mux returns a hardware value you can wire or nest. when is a statement that connects sinks.

practice.q: What does MuxLookup pick with?
options: A key matched against a Seq of key -> value pairs
practice.answer: A key matched against a Seq of key -> value pairs
practice.why: MuxLookup(sel, default)(Seq(...)) is a lookup mux. Unmatched keys give the default.

practice.q: What is switch / is?
options: A multi-way when over a hardware selector
A Scala match that deletes unused arms at elaboration
practice.answer: A multi-way when over a hardware selector
practice.why: Every is arm is hardware. The selector chooses which connections apply.

practice.q: After a default io.y := 0.U and an is arm that assigns io.y, when the key misses, what is driven?
practice.answer: The default 0.U
practice.why: An unmatched switch leaves earlier connections in place. Last-connect-wins is still conditional.

lessons.title: Vec and VecInit
lessons.summary: Bundles of wires indexed by a signal.

sections.p: A Vec is a fixed-length collection of the same hardware type. Vec(4, UInt(8.W)) is four 8-bit unsigned wires. Indexing with a hardware UInt builds a mux (read) or a demux of writes. A Scala Int index is resolved at elaboration and picks one element with no mux.
sections.code:
val banks = Wire(Vec(4, UInt(8.W)))
banks(0) := 1.U
banks(1) := 2.U
banks(2) := 3.U
banks(3) := 4.U
io.y := banks(io.sel)

sections.p: VecInit(1.U, 2.U, 3.U) builds a Vec already connected to those values. A Scala for over 0 until n at elaboration can fill a Vec element by element — that loop runs once while the circuit is built, not every clock.

practice.q: What is Vec(4, UInt(8.W))?
practice.answer: Four 8-bit unsigned elements
practice.why: Vec(n, T) is n copies of type T in one hardware collection.

practice.q: Indexing a Vec with a hardware UInt builds what?
options: A Scala for-loop that runs every clock
Nothing; only Int indexes are allowed
practice.answer: A mux (or demux of writes)
practice.why: A signal index must pick among elements in the circuit. A literal Int index is wired at elaboration.

practice.q: What does VecInit(1.U, 2.U, 3.U) do?
options: Builds a Vec already driven by those literals
Allocates empty Wires you must connect later
practice.answer: Builds a Vec already driven by those literals
practice.why: VecInit connects each argument to an element. It is a handy ROM or constant table.

practice.q: A Scala for (i <- 0 until 4) { banks(i) := ... } runs when?
options: Never; for is banned in Chisel
practice.answer: Once, at elaboration
practice.why: Scala for unrolls into hardware. The circuit then has four connections, not a looping CPU.

practice.q: Why can a Vec replace a pile of MuxLookup arms?
options: A hardware index into the Vec is already a mux
practice.answer: A hardware index into the Vec is already a mux
practice.why: banks(io.sel) is the lookup. Tables of constants are often VecInit.

lessons.title: Mem and SyncReadMem
lessons.summary: Addressable storage, async and sync read.

sections.p: Mem(n, T) is a memory of n elements of type T. A write is mem.write(addr, data) or mem(addr) := data. A combinational (asynchronous) read is mem.read(addr) or mem(addr): the data can change in the same cycle as the address.

SyncReadMem models a synchronous-read RAM: you present an address, and the data appears on the next clock. That matches most FPGA block RAMs. Mixing up Mem and SyncReadMem is a common source of off-by-one-cycle bugs in testbenches.

practice.q: What is Mem(32, UInt(8.W))?
options: A Vec that cannot be written
practice.answer: 32 addressable 8-bit elements
practice.why: Mem is a memory array. The first argument is the depth.

practice.q: When can a Mem async read return new data?
options: In the same cycle as the address
practice.answer: In the same cycle as the address
practice.why: Combinational read follows the address immediately. SyncReadMem waits a clock.

practice.q: What does SyncReadMem model better than Mem?
options: FPGA block RAMs with a one-cycle read latency
practice.answer: FPGA block RAMs with a one-cycle read latency
practice.why: Synchronous read matches the hardware. Expect data on the cycle after the address.

practice.q: How do you write Mem under a condition?
practice.answer: when (io.wen) { mem.write(addr, data) }
practice.why: Guard the write with when so the memory is not written every cycle.

practice.q: Why might a testbench that worked with Mem fail after switching to SyncReadMem?
options: The read data arrives one cycle later
practice.answer: The read data arrives one cycle later
practice.why: The address-to-data path gained a register. Checks must wait a clock.

sections.p: Flipped(bundle) swaps every Input and Output inside a bundle. A child module’s producer port is the flip of the parent’s consumer view, so you connect them field-by-field (or with <>) without renaming directions by hand.

Decoupled(T) is a ready–valid handshake carrying a payload of type T. The producer drives valid and bits; the consumer drives ready. A transfer happens when both valid and ready are high in the same cycle. Irrevocable is the stricter cousin that promises bits will not change while valid stays high and ready is low.
sink <> source bulk-connects matching fields, flipping directions as needed. Forgetting ready (tying it high forever) can hide back-pressure bugs; forgetting valid stalls the consumer forever.

practice.q: What does Flipped do to a bundle?
options: Swaps every Input and Output inside it
practice.answer: Swaps every Input and Output inside it
practice.why: Flip lines a producer up with a consumer without rewriting each field.

practice.q: Who drives Decoupled.valid and bits?
practice.answer: The producer
practice.why: valid and bits come from the source. ready comes from the sink.

practice.q: When does a Decoupled transfer occur?
options: When valid and ready are both high
When valid is high, ignoring ready
practice.answer: When valid and ready are both high
practice.why: Both sides must agree in the same cycle. That is the handshake.

practice.q: Who drives Decoupled.ready?
practice.answer: The consumer
practice.why: ready is back-pressure from the sink. Producers must respect it.

practice.q: What is <> between two bundles?
options: A bulk connect of matching fields
practice.answer: A bulk connect of matching fields
practice.why: <> wires corresponding names and handles flipped directions.

lessons.title: State machines with Enum
lessons.summary: Named states, switch, and next-state logic.

sections.p: Enum(n) (or ChiselEnum in newer code) gives n distinct state values. Hold the current state in a RegInit, then use switch (state) both to decide outputs and to choose the next state. The next-state assignment is just another connection into that register.

Set defaults before the switch (io.finished := false.B, and so on) so every state has a defined drive. Only the active state overrides what it cares about. That pattern avoids latches and missing connections.

practice.q: What does Enum(3) provide?
practice.answer: Three distinct state values
practice.why: Enum(n) is a list of n unique UInt constants for states.

practice.q: Where does the current state live?
options: In a Reg (often RegInit to the idle value)
In Scala var that changes every clock by itself
practice.answer: In a Reg (often RegInit to the idle value)
practice.why: State must survive between clocks. A register holds it.

practice.q: How do you move from one state to another?
options: Connect the next value into the state register inside switch / when
Change Enum at elaboration each cycle
practice.answer: Connect the next value into the state register inside switch / when
practice.why: state := load is next-state logic. The register updates on the clock.

practice.q: Why assign default outputs before switch?
options: So every signal is driven even when a state does not mention it
practice.answer: So every signal is driven even when a state does not mention it
practice.why: Defaults plus overrides keep the circuit fully connected and predictable.

practice.q: Is the next-state assignment combinatorial or registered?
options: The logic is combinatorial into the Reg; the Reg updates on the clock
The state changes during elaboration only
practice.answer: The logic is combinatorial into the Reg; the Reg updates on the clock
practice.why: switch builds muxes into the Reg’s input. The stored state flips on the edge.

lessons.title: Project: a nut sorter
lessons.summary: An FSM that tallies acorns and walnuts on a Decoupled input.

sections.p: A tiny sorter accepts a stream of nut codes on a Decoupled input: 0 means acorn, 1 means walnut, and any other code is ignored. While io.start is high the machine sits in run, handshake-accepting each beat and adding one to the matching counter. When start falls it moves to report, freezes the totals on the outputs, then returns to idle. The sketch uses Enum, when, registers and a ready–valid port together — the same pieces as a small streaming peripheral.

Add a hazelnut code, reject beats with an error flag instead of ignoring them, or replace the two counters with a Vec(3, UInt(8.W)) indexed by the code. On a real Chisel install, drive in from a testbench poke/peek loop and check done.

practice.q: When does the sorter accept an input beat?
options: In run, when in.valid and in.ready are both high (in.fire)
practice.answer: In run, when in.valid and in.ready are both high (in.fire)
practice.why: ready is tied true only in run. fire is the Chisel helper for valid && ready.

practice.q: What happens to a beat whose bits are 2.U?
options: It is accepted but neither counter moves
It forces state back to idle
practice.answer: It is accepted but neither counter moves
practice.why: ready is high, so the handshake completes; only 0 and 1 increment.

practice.q: When are the counters cleared?
options: On the idle → run transition when start rises
practice.answer: On the idle → run transition when start rises
practice.why: The idle arm zeroes both registers before entering run.

practice.q: Why is io.in a Flipped(Decoupled(...))?
options: The sorter is the consumer: it sees ready as an Output and valid/bits as Inputs
Flip makes the port a register
Decoupled cannot be an Input otherwise
practice.answer: The sorter is the consumer: it sees ready as an Output and valid/bits as Inputs
practice.why: Decoupled’s default view is producer-sided. Flipped swaps it for a sink.

practice.q: What does the report state do?
options: Holds done high and shows the totals until start is low, then returns to idle
practice.answer: Holds done high and shows the totals until start is low, then returns to idle
practice.why: report freezes the result on the outputs; leaving start low sends the FSM home.
